questions.question: What is the difference between INNER JOIN, LEFT JOIN, and RIGHT JOIN in SQL?
questions.title: INNER JOIN vs LEFT JOIN vs RIGHT JOIN in SQL
questions.direct_answer: **INNER JOIN** returns only rows that match in both tables. **LEFT JOIN** returns all rows from the left table plus matches from the right (NULLs where none match). **RIGHT JOIN** is the mirror — all rows from the right table plus left matches.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know which rows each join keeps and where NULLs appear.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Adding a WHERE filter on the right table after a LEFT JOIN, silently turning it into an INNER JOIN.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that filtering the right table in WHERE (not ON) drops the unmatched left rows.

sections.title: INNER, LEFT, and RIGHT JOIN
sections.content:
A **JOIN** combines rows from two tables on a matching condition. **INNER JOIN** keeps only rows that match in *both* tables. **LEFT JOIN** (left outer) keeps *all* left-table rows and fills right-side columns with **NULL** when there's no match. **RIGHT JOIN** does the same from the right table's side.

The fresher trap: after a LEFT JOIN, a `WHERE right.col = x` condition removes the NULL rows — turning your LEFT JOIN back into an INNER JOIN without you noticing.

sections.title: Join Types Compared
sections.content:
| Join | Rows returned | Unmatched rows | NULLs appear |
|---|---|---|---|
| INNER | only matches in both | dropped | never |
| LEFT | all left + matched right | left kept | right columns |
| RIGHT | all right + matched left | right kept | left columns |
| FULL OUTER | all rows from both | both kept | either side |

sections.title: Customers ↔ Orders Relationship
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart LR C[customers
id PK
name] -->|one| O[orders
id PK
customer_id FK
total] O -->|many| C C -.INNER.-> M[matched only] C -.LEFT.-> A[all customers
even with no orders] ```

sections.title: INNER vs LEFT and the result
sections.content:
```sql
-- INNER: only customers who have orders
SELECT c.name, o.total
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id;

-- LEFT: every customer, NULL total when no orders
SELECT c.name, o.total
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id;
```

Sample output (LEFT JOIN):

| name | total |
|---|---|
| Ravi | 1200 |
| Neha | NULL |

*Neha has no orders, so she still appears with a NULL total.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **LEFT JOIN + WHERE on right table**: `WHERE o.total > 0` drops the NULL rows — put the filter in the `ON` clause to keep them.
- **Confusing direction**: LEFT keeps the first/left table; RIGHT keeps the second.
- **Forgetting the ON condition**: omitting it (in some dialects) yields a Cartesian product.
- **Expecting NULLs from INNER JOIN**: INNER never produces NULL fill rows.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **INNER** = matches in both tables only.
- **LEFT** = all left rows + matched right (NULLs otherwise).
- **RIGHT** = mirror of LEFT.
- **Filter the right table in `ON`, not `WHERE`**, to keep a LEFT JOIN.
- **INNER JOIN never produces NULL** fill rows.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: A join combines rows from two tables based on a matching condition, and the three you use most are inner, left, and right. An inner join returns only the rows that have a match in both tables, so if a customer has no orders, that customer simply doesn't appear. A left join, sometimes called left outer join, returns every row from the left table plus the matching rows from the right, and where there's no match it fills the right-side columns with NULL. So with customers left-joined to orders, even a customer with zero orders shows up, just with a NULL total. A right join is the exact mirror: all rows from the right table plus matches from the left. The trap that catches a lot of freshers is mixing a left join with a WHERE filter on the right table. If I do a left join and then write WHERE order total greater than zero, those NULL rows fail the condition and get dropped, which silently turns my left join back into an inner join. The fix is to move that condition into the ON clause instead of WHERE, so the unmatched left rows are preserved. So the mental model is: inner keeps intersections, left and right keep one whole side, and where you put a filter, ON versus WHERE, decides whether the outer rows survive.

What is a FULL OUTER JOIN?

questions.question: What is a CROSS JOIN in SQL?
questions.title: CROSS JOIN in SQL — Cartesian Product
questions.direct_answer: A **CROSS JOIN** produces the **Cartesian product** — every row of the first table paired with every row of the second, so M rows × N rows = M×N results. It has no ON condition and is used deliberately for combinations (e.g., sizes × colors), or appears accidentally from a missing join condition.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the Cartesian product and its row-count explosion.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Producing a CROSS JOIN by accident via a forgotten ON/WHERE condition.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a legit use (generating combinations / calendars) and the accidental-blowup warning.

sections.title: What a CROSS JOIN Does
sections.content:
A **CROSS JOIN** pairs every row of one table with every row of another — the **Cartesian product**. With 4 sizes and 3 colors you get 12 combinations. Unlike other joins, it has **no `ON` condition**.

It's occasionally intentional (build all size×color variants, generate a date grid), but it's more often an **accident**: forget the join condition and a 10,000-row table joined to another 10,000-row table explodes to 100 million rows.

sections.title: CROSS JOIN at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|What|~Cartesian product|every row x every row|M x N result rows|no ON condition
emerald|Good use|~generate combinations|sizes x colors|date x store grids|test data
rose|Accidental|~missing join condition|row count explodes|10k x 10k = 100M|server slows or crashes
amber|Control|~be deliberate|use CROSS JOIN keyword|or add proper ON|verify row count

sections.title: Intentional CROSS JOIN
sections.content:
```sql
-- all size + color combinations
SELECT s.size, c.color
FROM sizes s
CROSS JOIN colors c;
```

Sample output (2 sizes × 2 colors = 4 rows):

| size | color |
|---|---|
| S | Red |
| S | Blue |
| M | Red |
| M | Blue |

*No matching condition — every size is paired with every color.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Accidental Cartesian product**: listing two tables in FROM without a join condition produces a CROSS JOIN.
- **Underestimating the blowup**: M×N grows fast — always sanity-check the expected row count.
- **Using it where INNER fits**: if rows should match on a key, you want INNER JOIN, not CROSS.
- **Memory/timeout risk**: large cross joins can exhaust memory or time out.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **CROSS JOIN** = Cartesian product, M×N rows.
- **No `ON` condition** — every pair is produced.
- **Intentional uses**: combinations, calendars, test grids.
- **Accidental cause**: a forgotten join condition.
- **Watch the row count** — it explodes quickly.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: A cross join produces the Cartesian product of two tables, which means it pairs every row of the first table with every row of the second. So if I have four sizes and three colors, a cross join gives me twelve rows, one for each combination. Unlike inner or outer joins, a cross join has no ON condition, because there's nothing to match on; the point is to generate all combinations. There are legitimate uses for it: building every size-and-color product variant, generating a grid of dates against stores for a report, or creating test data. But honestly, the more common way you meet a cross join is by accident. If you list two tables in the FROM clause and forget the join condition, many databases happily give you a cross join. That's dangerous because the row count multiplies: a ten thousand row table crossed with another ten thousand row table is a hundred million rows, which can slow the server to a crawl or run out of memory. So my rule is, whenever I actually want a cross join, I write the CROSS JOIN keyword explicitly to show it's deliberate, and whenever I see a surprisingly huge result set, the first thing I check is whether I accidentally dropped a join condition.

questions.question: What is a self-join in SQL and when would you use it?
questions.title: Self-Join in SQL — Joining a Table to Itself
questions.direct_answer: A **self-join** joins a table to **itself**, using table aliases to treat it as two logical tables. It models hierarchical or comparison relationships within one table — classically *employee → manager*, where both live in the same `employees` table.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can join a table to itself with aliases for hierarchical data.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting aliases, or using INNER (which drops top-level rows that have no parent).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use LEFT self-join so the CEO (no manager) still appears.

sections.title: What a Self-Join Is
sections.content:
A **self-join** is just a regular join where both sides are the **same table**. You give the table two **aliases** so the query can treat it as two copies and relate rows to other rows in the same table.

The textbook case is an `employees` table where each row has a `manager_id` pointing to another row's `id`. To list each employee with their manager's name, you join `employees e` to `employees m` on `e.manager_id = m.id`. Use a **LEFT** self-join so the top boss (no manager) still shows up.

sections.title: Self-Join at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|What|~table joined to itself|two aliases needed|e and m|relates rows to rows
emerald|Use cases|~hierarchy + comparison|employee -> manager|categories -> parent|find duplicates
amber|Aliases|~mandatory|distinguish the copies|e.col vs m.col|else ambiguous
rose|LEFT vs INNER|~keep top rows|INNER drops the CEO|LEFT keeps no-parent rows|pick LEFT for hierarchy

sections.title: Employee → manager self-join
sections.content:
```sql
SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id
ORDER BY manager;
```

Sample output:

| employee | manager |
|---|---|
| Asha | NULL |
| Ravi | Asha |
| Neha | Asha |

*Asha is the CEO — her `manager_id` is NULL, so the LEFT join keeps her with a NULL manager.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **No aliases**: the database can't tell which copy you mean — always alias both.
- **INNER for hierarchy**: drops rows with no parent (the CEO). Use LEFT.
- **Infinite logic for deep trees**: a single self-join is one level deep; deep hierarchies need recursive CTEs.
- **Confusing the join column direction**: `e.manager_id = m.id`, not the reverse.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Self-join** = a table joined to itself via aliases.
- **Aliases are required** to disambiguate the two copies.
- **Classic use**: employee→manager and other hierarchies.
- **LEFT self-join** keeps top-level rows (no parent).
- **Deep trees** need recursive CTEs, not a single self-join.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: A self-join is when you join a table to itself. It sounds odd at first, but it's just a normal join where both sides happen to be the same table, and you use aliases so SQL can treat it as two logical copies. The classic example is an employees table where every row has a manager_id that points to another row's id in the same table. If I want to list each employee next to their manager's name, I join employees aliased as e to employees aliased as m, on e dot manager_id equals m dot id. The aliases are mandatory, because without them the database can't tell which copy of the column you mean. One important choice is inner versus left. If I use an inner join, the very top of the hierarchy, say the CEO who has no manager, gets dropped because there's no matching manager row. So for hierarchies I use a left join, which keeps that top row with a NULL manager. Self-joins are great for hierarchical data and for comparisons within a table, like finding employees who earn more than their manager, or detecting duplicate rows. The one limitation is that a single self-join only goes one level deep; for arbitrarily deep trees, like a full org chart, you'd switch to a recursive common table expression.

followup_questions: How do you query a hierarchy more than one level deep?
Why use LEFT JOIN instead of INNER for a self-join?
How would you find employees earning more than their manager?

questions.question: What is the N+1 query problem and how does it relate to SQL joins?
questions.title: N+1 Query Problem in SQL and ORM
questions.direct_answer: The **N+1 problem** is firing one query to fetch N parent rows, then one extra query per parent to fetch its children — 1 + N round-trips that hammer the database. The fix is a single **JOIN** (or `JOIN FETCH` in JPA) that loads parents and children in one query.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can recognize the N+1 pattern and fix it with a join.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Looping over results and querying inside the loop (lazy loading per entity).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name JPA JOIN FETCH / @EntityGraph as the ORM-level fix and mention round-trip latency.

sections.title: The N+1 Query Problem
sections.content:
The **N+1 problem** happens when code fetches a list of N parents with one query, then issues **one more query per parent** to load related data — totaling **1 + N** queries. With 100 orders, that's 101 round-trips; each network round-trip adds latency, so the page crawls.

The fix is to fetch everything in **one query using a JOIN**. In JPA/Hibernate, where lazy loading triggers the extra queries, you use **`JOIN FETCH`** or an **`@EntityGraph`** to load parents and children together.

sections.title: N+1 at a Glance
sections.content:
rose|Symptom|~1 + N queries|1 query for parents|N queries for children|round-trips explode
blue|Cause|~query inside a loop|lazy load per entity|order.getCustomer()|fine in tests, bad at scale
emerald|Fix|~one JOIN|load related data together|JPA JOIN FETCH|or @EntityGraph
amber|Cost|~latency, not CPU|each round-trip adds time|network bound|join cuts it to one

sections.title: N+1 vs Single JOIN
sections.content:
| Aspect | N+1 (lazy loop) | Single JOIN |
|---|---|---|
| Queries | 1 + N | 1 |
| Round-trips | grows with N | constant |
| Latency | high (network per row) | low |
| JPA fix | default lazy loading | `JOIN FETCH` / `@EntityGraph` |

sections.title: N+1: a query per parent
sections.content:
```sql
-- 1 query for the orders
SELECT id, customer_id FROM orders;          -- returns 100 rows

-- then, in app code, ONE query per order (100 more):
SELECT name FROM customers WHERE id = ?;     -- x100
-- total: 1 + 100 = 101 queries
```

sections.title: One JOIN loads everything
sections.content:
```sql
-- a single query joins orders to customers
SELECT o.id, c.name
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id;    -- 1 query total
```

In JPA: `@Query("SELECT o FROM Order o JOIN FETCH o.customer")` loads orders and their customers in one round-trip instead of 1 + N.

sections.title: When N+1 Bites
sections.content:
It shows up whenever you **iterate a collection and access a lazy relationship inside the loop** — rendering a list of orders and reading `order.getCustomer().getName()` for each. It's invisible in tests with 2 rows and catastrophic with 10,000.

Fix it with a JOIN (`JOIN FETCH`/`@EntityGraph`) when you know you'll need the related data; keep lazy loading when you usually don't.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **N+1** = 1 parent query + N child queries.
- **Cause**: querying inside a loop / lazy loading per entity.
- **Fix**: a single JOIN to load related data together.
- **JPA fix**: `JOIN FETCH` or `@EntityGraph`.
- **Cost is latency** — each round-trip adds network time.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: The N plus one problem is one of the most common database performance bugs, and interviewers love it. It happens when you run one query to fetch a list of N parent records, and then, usually inside a loop, you run one more query for each parent to load its related data. So one query plus N queries equals N plus one total. With a hundred orders where I fetch each order's customer separately, that's a hundred and one trips to the database. Each trip carries network latency, so even if every query is individually fast, the page feels slow because of all the round-trips. The fix is to load everything in a single query using a join. Instead of fetching orders and then looking up each customer, I join orders to customers and get it all back at once. In JPA or Hibernate this problem is especially sneaky because lazy loading triggers those extra queries automatically the moment you touch a related entity inside a loop. The ORM-level fix is JOIN FETCH in your JPQL, or an EntityGraph, which tells Hibernate to fetch the parents and their children together in one query. The mental model I keep is: if I know I'll need the related data for every row, I join it up front; if I rarely need it, lazy loading is fine.

followup_questions: How does JPA JOIN FETCH solve the N+1 problem?
What is the difference between lazy and eager loading?

questions.question: What is the difference between using ON and WHERE in a JOIN?
questions.title: ON vs WHERE in SQL JOINs
questions.direct_answer: In a join, the **ON** clause defines how rows *match*; the **WHERE** clause filters the *result* afterward. For INNER JOIN they're often interchangeable, but for **OUTER JOINs** they differ sharply: a condition on the outer table in WHERE drops the NULL-filled rows, while in ON it keeps them.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know ON vs WHERE differ for outer joins.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Filtering the right table in WHERE after a LEFT JOIN and accidentally making it INNER.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain ON runs during the join, WHERE runs after, so outer rows survive only if filtered in ON.

sections.title: ON vs WHERE in Joins
sections.content: **`ON`** specifies the *join condition* — how rows from the two tables are matched. **`WHERE`** filters the *combined result* after the join is formed. For an **INNER JOIN** the distinction rarely matters because both run before any rows survive. For an **OUTER JOIN** it's critical: outer (NULL-filled) rows are created by the join, then a `WHERE` condition on the outer table can throw them away — a `ON` condition won't.

sections.title: ON vs WHERE at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|ON|~match condition|runs during the join|keeps outer rows|defines pairing
emerald|WHERE|~result filter|runs after the join|can drop outer rows|filters final set
amber|INNER JOIN|~mostly equivalent|either place works|readability choice|
rose|OUTER JOIN|~choice matters|filter in ON keeps NULL rows|filter in WHERE drops them|LEFT can become INNER

sections.title: ON vs WHERE
sections.content:
| Aspect | ON | WHERE |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | match rows | filter result |
| Runs | during the join | after the join |
| INNER JOIN | same effect... | ...as ON |
| LEFT JOIN | keeps unmatched left rows | can drop unmatched rows |
| Filter right table | preserves outer rows | turns LEFT into INNER |

sections.title: WHERE on the right table breaks the outer join
sections.content:
```sql
-- intent: all customers, plus their 2026 orders
SELECT c.name, o.total
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.order_year = 2026;
-- BUG: customers with no 2026 order have NULL order_year,
-- which fails the WHERE, so they vanish -> effectively INNER JOIN
```

sections.title: Move the filter into ON to keep all customers
sections.content:
```sql
SELECT c.name, o.total
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
  ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.order_year = 2026;
-- now every customer appears; non-2026 customers get NULL total
```

Sample output:

| name | total |
|---|---|
| Ravi | 1200 |
| Neha | NULL |

sections.title: When It Matters
sections.content:
With **INNER JOIN**, put the matching condition in ON and filters in WHERE — readability over correctness, since both work.

With **OUTER JOIN**, decide intent: a condition that should *still allow* unmatched outer rows belongs in **ON**; a condition that should *remove* rows from the final result belongs in **WHERE**.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **ON** matches rows; **WHERE** filters the result.
- **INNER JOIN**: ON vs WHERE are usually equivalent.
- **OUTER JOIN**: a WHERE on the outer table drops NULL rows.
- **Keep outer rows** by filtering in ON, not WHERE.
- **ON runs during the join, WHERE runs after.**

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: In a join, ON and WHERE do two different jobs. The ON clause defines how the two tables match up, the join condition. The WHERE clause filters the combined result after the join has already been formed. For an inner join, the difference rarely matters in practice, because rows only survive if they match and pass the filter, so you can put the condition in either place. But for an outer join, like a left join, the difference is huge. A left join first creates rows for every left-table row, filling the right side with NULLs where there's no match. If I then add a WHERE condition on a right-table column, those NULL rows fail the condition and get removed, which silently turns my left join into an inner join. The classic example is all customers plus their twenty twenty-six orders: if I filter order year equals twenty twenty-six in WHERE, customers with no order that year disappear. The fix is to move that condition into the ON clause, so it becomes part of the match rather than a post-filter. Then every customer still appears, and the ones without a matching order just get a NULL total. So the rule I follow is: a condition that should still allow unmatched outer rows goes in ON; a condition meant to remove rows from the final result goes in WHERE.

followup_questions: Why does a WHERE clause turn a LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN?
Are ON and WHERE equivalent for INNER JOIN?

ON is the join condition applied during the join itself — rows that do not match still appear in the result with NULLs. questions.question: What is a FULL OUTER JOIN and how is it simulated in MySQL?
questions.title: FULL OUTER JOIN in SQL
questions.direct_answer: A **FULL OUTER JOIN** returns all rows from both tables — matched rows joined, plus unmatched rows from each side with NULLs on the missing side. MySQL has no native FULL OUTER JOIN, so you simulate it with a **`UNION` of a LEFT JOIN and a RIGHT JOIN**.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know FULL OUTER JOIN semantics and the MySQL UNION workaround.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming MySQL supports FULL OUTER JOIN, or using UNION ALL (which duplicates matched rows).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use UNION (de-dupes) and note the LEFT + RIGHT-with-NULL-filter pattern.

sections.title: FULL OUTER JOIN and the MySQL Workaround
sections.content:
A **FULL OUTER JOIN** keeps everything: rows that match in both tables, plus unmatched rows from the **left** (NULLs on the right) and unmatched rows from the **right** (NULLs on the left). It's how you find records present in either table but not necessarily both.

Postgres and SQL Server support it natively. **MySQL does not**, so you simulate it by combining a `LEFT JOIN` and a `RIGHT JOIN` with **`UNION`** (which removes the duplicate matched rows).

sections.title: FULL OUTER JOIN at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|What|~all rows, both sides|matched rows joined|unmatched left + NULL|unmatched right + NULL
emerald|Native|~Postgres, SQL Server|FULL OUTER JOIN keyword|one statement|
amber|MySQL|~no native support|LEFT JOIN UNION RIGHT JOIN|UNION de-dupes|or filter right-only side
rose|UNION vs UNION ALL|~de-dupe matters|UNION removes duplicates|UNION ALL keeps them|use UNION here

sections.title: Native vs MySQL-simulated FULL OUTER JOIN
sections.content:
```sql
-- Postgres / SQL Server (native)
SELECT c.name, o.total
FROM customers c
FULL OUTER JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id;

-- MySQL (simulated with UNION)
SELECT c.name, o.total FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
UNION
SELECT c.name, o.total FROM customers c
RIGHT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id;
```

Sample output:

| name | total |
|---|---|
| Ravi | 1200 |
| Neha | NULL |
| NULL | 50 |

*Neha has no order; the last row is an order with no matching customer.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Assuming MySQL supports it**: it doesn't — use the UNION pattern.
- **`UNION ALL` instead of `UNION`**: matched rows appear twice; UNION removes the duplicates.
- **Mismatched columns**: both SELECTs in the UNION must have the same columns in the same order.
- **Confusing with INNER**: FULL OUTER keeps non-matching rows; INNER drops them.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **FULL OUTER JOIN** = all rows from both tables, NULLs where unmatched.
- **Native** in Postgres/SQL Server; **absent in MySQL**.
- **MySQL pattern**: `LEFT JOIN UNION RIGHT JOIN`.
- **Use `UNION`** (not `UNION ALL`) to de-dupe matched rows.
- **Both UNION halves** must select identical columns.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: A full outer join returns every row from both tables. Rows that match are joined together, rows that exist only in the left table come back with NULLs on the right, and rows that exist only in the right table come back with NULLs on the left. It's the join you reach for when you want to see everything from either side, like reconciling two lists to find records that are in one but not the other. Postgres and SQL Server support full outer join natively with the keyword, so it's one statement. MySQL, though, doesn't have a native full outer join, which is a favorite interview gotcha. The standard way to simulate it in MySQL is to take a left join and union it with a right join. The left join gives you all left rows plus matches, the right join gives you all right rows plus matches, and UNION combines them. The important detail is to use UNION, not UNION ALL, because UNION removes duplicates, and the matched rows would otherwise appear twice, once from each half. Both halves of the union also have to select the same columns in the same order. So the short version is: full outer join means all rows from both sides with NULLs where there's no match, it's native in Postgres and SQL Server, and in MySQL you fake it with a left join UNION a right join.

beats.content: FULL OUTER JOIN returns all rows from both tables. Where a match exists, the columns from both sides are filled in. Where there is no match on either side, NULLs appear for the missing columns. It is essentially LEFT JOIN and RIGHT JOIN combined. PostgreSQL, Oracle, and SQL Server support this natively.

non-obvious: MySQL does not have FULL OUTER JOIN syntax. To get the same result, you combine a LEFT JOIN and a RIGHT JOIN using UNION. You use UNION rather than UNION ALL because UNION removes duplicates — the rows that matched on both sides would otherwise appear twice.
